rationale: Start with a broad, mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible while revealing overall retention spread and any severe crowding. This gives a balanced first map of the mixture before optimizing selectivity or gradient steepness.

All compounds eluted early with baseline resolution, so the main opportunity is to lower the time penalty by using a weaker final solvent and longer gradient to spread the crowded middle cluster while keeping all 10 peaks on-scale. This probes whether we can maintain full resolution with a lower phi1 that still elutes the last peak before 42 min.

The first run already had perfect resolution, so we should now push to reduce analysis time rather than increase separation. A steeper but not extreme gradient should compress the chromatogram and test whether all 10 compounds still remain baseline resolved with a lower time penalty.

Run 3 is already near-optimal, with only the 6/7 pair slightly under baseline resolution. A small increase in final strength at the same gradient time may selectively shift the crowded mid-eluting cluster and improve that pair while keeping the run short and time penalty at zero.

The limiting issue is the slightly compressed 6/7 pair in the fast 12 min gradient, so a modest increase in gradient time at the successful phi range should improve mid-gradient selectivity without incurring a time penalty. This is a local refinement around the current best method.

Since a longer gradient improved the 6/7 pair but added enough time to lower CRF, the next best local move is to keep the short 12 min gradient and slightly weaken phi1. That should expand the crowded middle region and may lift the 6/7 resolution above the current 1.36 while preserving a zero time penalty.

Since 0.75/12/40 already gives the maximum score, the only useful exploration is a very small step nearby to test whether the optimum sits on a plateau. Lowering phi1 one grid step should slightly expand the crowded middle region while likely keeping all peaks before the time penalty threshold.

The optimum may still be broad, and changing phi0 can alter early-gradient selectivity differently from changing phi1. Lowering phi0 one step while keeping the proven phi1 and tG tests whether the critical 6/7 region can be preserved or improved without introducing a time penalty.

With the maximum already achieved, the remaining valuable information is whether a nearby temperature change offers an equally good or broader optimum. Lowering temperature by one step can subtly change selectivity in the crowded 6/7 region while staying close to the proven fast method.

Temperature clearly affects selectivity strongly, and 35 C worsened a different pair, so the complementary test is one step higher than the optimum. This checks whether 40 C is a sharp maximum or whether a slightly hotter method preserves full resolution with similar speed.

Temperature excursions confirmed 40 C is best, so the last nearby lever worth probing is a slightly higher starting organic fraction. Raising phi0 one step may alter the crowded early-middle section differently from phi1 while likely keeping the run within the zero-penalty window.

We now know there is at least a small plateau at the maximum, so the next efficient probe is to continue stepping phi0 upward while keeping the successful phi1, tG, and temperature fixed. This tests whether the max-CRF region extends further and could support an even stronger starting condition without losing baseline resolution.

The maximum-score region includes phi0 0.15 at phi1 0.75, so a one-step lower phi1 from that point is the cleanest nearby test of the plateau. This may keep full resolution while showing whether the optimum extends diagonally toward weaker ending strength.

We have mapped the weaker side of the optimum around phi0 0.15, so the complementary one-step stronger phi1 test will define the local plateau width on the high-strength side. This should show whether the maximum is centered near phi1 0.75 or whether equally good conditions extend upward.

The current maximum forms a ridge near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.75, so a diagonal test toward lower phi0 and higher phi1 helps define that ridge boundary. This nearby condition could reveal whether compensating phi0/phi1 shifts preserve the top-scoring selectivity.

We already have multiple 1.000 methods, so the only remaining useful question is whether the same selectivity survives a shorter run. Reducing tG by one step at a max-scoring composition directly tests whether the plateau extends to even faster gradients without sacrificing the critical middle-pair resolution.

Shortening to 10 min hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so the useful opposite probe is a modestly longer gradient at the same max-scoring composition. This maps the robustness of the optimum and checks whether extra margin in resolution is available with only a small time cost.

A large temperature effect is evident, but only 35 and 45 C were tested near the optimum; a lower endpoint can reveal whether selectivity changes nonlinearly and whether a different pair becomes limiting. This is a deliberate boundary probe to complete the temperature map around the max-scoring region.

Since 25–45 C shows a strong, nonmonotonic temperature dependence and 40 C is optimal, the last informative boundary check is the high extreme. Testing 60 C will complete the temperature profile and confirm whether the max region is isolated around 40 C or if selectivity recovers at higher temperature.

Lower temperature at 12 min caused severe coelution, suggesting the cooler condition needs a shallower gradient to recover selectivity. This targeted combination tests whether the 35 C selectivity can be rescued enough to approach the optimum while remaining reasonably fast.

At 35 C the main failure is the 5/6 pair, and increasing phi0 shifted the pattern favorably at 40 C without hurting runtime too much. This targeted follow-up tests whether the higher starting strength can relieve that low-temperature crowding better than the 0.10/0.75/14/35 condition.

With the maximum already secured, the best remaining use of injections is mapping the nearby ridge in composition space. This diagonal move to lower phi0 and phi1 explores whether a broader lower-strength region still gives full resolution with acceptable runtime.

A zero-penalty maximum was achieved at phi1 0.75, while phi1 0.70 and lower start to incur time cost; testing 0.65 at the proven phi0 and temperature sharpens that boundary. This final local probe helps define how quickly CRF falls on the weaker-gradient side of the optimum.

The maximum plateau includes phi0 0.15 at phi1 0.75, so pairing that higher phi0 with the weaker phi1 0.65 tests whether increased starting strength offsets the added retention time. This completes the local composition map on the low-phi1 side near the best region.

For the final injection, probe the remaining untested corner adjacent to the best region: higher phi0 combined with slightly lower phi1. This completes the local map around the 1.000 plateau and tests whether the favorable higher-start composition can tolerate a weaker endpoint without losing too much CRF.
